  1. 1

    A line passes through (−3,2)(-3, 2)(−3,2) and (1,10)(1, 10)(1,10). What is its slope?

    Answer choices for question 1

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Divides the run by the rise, reporting 48\tfrac{4}{8}84​ in place of 84\tfrac{8}{4}48​.

    You chose C: Stops at the rise 10−210 - 210−2 and never divides by the run.

    You chose D: Subtracts the yyy-values in one order and the xxx-values in the other, computing 10−2−3−1\tfrac{10 - 2}{-3 - 1}−3−110−2​.

    Slope is rise over run, with both differences taken in the same order.

    m=10−21−(−3)=84=2m = \frac{10 - 2}{1 - (-3)} = \frac{8}{4} = 2m=1−(−3)10−2​=48​=2

    The line climbs 222 units for every 111 unit it runs to the right.

  2. 2

    What is the x-intercept of the graph of 5x−4y=405x - 4y = 405x−4y=40?

    Answer choices for question 2

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Sets x=0x = 0x=0 rather than y=0y = 0y=0, which locates the crossing of the other axis.

    You chose B: Sets y=0y = 0y=0 correctly but then divides 404040 by −4-4−4, the coefficient of the term that was just zeroed out.

    You chose C: Solves for xxx correctly but writes the value in the second slot of the ordered pair.

    Every point of the x-axis has y=0y = 0y=0, so zero the yyy and solve for what is left.

    5x−4(0)=40,5x=40,x=85x - 4(0) = 40, \qquad 5x = 40, \qquad x = 85x−4(0)=40,5x=40,x=8

    The crossing is the point (8,0)(8, 0)(8,0). Zeroing xxx instead would have given the y-intercept (0,−10)(0, -10)(0,−10).

  3. 3

    What is the slope of the line y=7−3xy = 7 - 3xy=7−3x?

    Answer choices for question 3

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Takes the first number on the right as the slope, though it is the constant term.

    You chose C: Takes the coefficient of xxx but leaves behind the minus sign attached to it.

    You chose D: Takes the leading number as the slope and moves the xxx-term's minus sign onto it.

    Slope-intercept form lists the xxx-term first, so put the terms in that order before reading anything off.

    y=7−3x=−3x+7y = 7 - 3x = -3x + 7y=7−3x=−3x+7

    The number multiplying xxx is −3-3−3, so the slope is −3-3−3 and the line falls to the right. The 777 is the constant, which fixes the y-intercept at (0,7)(0, 7)(0,7).

  4. 4

    Which of these equations has a graph whose slope is undefined?

    Answer choices for question 4

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Swaps the flat case for the upright one; y=cy = cy=c locks the height, so its rise is 000 and its slope is 000.

    You chose B: Reads an equation with no constant term as one with no slope, though its slope is the coefficient 666.

    You chose D: Reads an equation carrying both letters as one with no single slope, though solving for yyy gives the slope −1-1−1.

    The slope formula returns no value only when its denominator, the run, is 000, and a run of 000 between two distinct points means both points sit in the same column. The equation x=−6x = -6x=−6 fixes the xxx-coordinate and leaves yyy free, so its graph is that column.

    m=rise−6−(−6)=rise0, which has no valuem = \frac{\text{rise}}{-6 - (-6)} = \frac{\text{rise}}{0}, \text{ which has no value}m=−6−(−6)rise​=0rise​, which has no value

    The equation y=−6y = -6y=−6 fixes the height instead, so its rise is 000 and its slope is the perfectly good number 000.

  5. 5

    Which of these points lies on the graph of 3x−2y=183x - 2y = 183x−2y=18?

    Answer choices for question 5

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Substitutes the coordinates in reverse, computing 3(4)−2(−3)3(4) - 2(-3)3(4)−2(−3) for the pair (−3,4)(-3, 4)(−3,4) and accepting the 181818 it produces.

    You chose C: Sets x=0x = 0x=0 and then solves −2y=18-2y = 18−2y=18 as though the coefficient were positive.

    You chose D: Sets y=0y = 0y=0 and divides 181818 by 222, the coefficient of the term just zeroed out, instead of by 333.

    A point is on the graph exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation, so substitute the first coordinate for xxx and the second for yyy.

    3(4)−2(−3)=12+6=183(4) - 2(-3) = 12 + 6 = 183(4)−2(−3)=12+6=18

    The two sides agree, so (4,−3)(4, -3)(4,−3) is on the line. The other three fail: (−3,4)(-3, 4)(−3,4) gives −17-17−17, (0,9)(0, 9)(0,9) gives −18-18−18, and (9,0)(9, 0)(9,0) gives 272727.

  6. 6

    A line has slope 35\tfrac{3}{5}53​. What is the slope of any line perpendicular to it?

    Answer choices for question 6

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Changes the sign without flipping the fraction, so the product of the slopes is −925-\tfrac{9}{25}−259​ rather than −1-1−1.

    You chose B: Flips the fraction without changing the sign, so the product of the slopes is +1+1+1 rather than −1-1−1.

    You chose D: Gives the slope of a parallel line, which copies the slope instead of reversing the direction.

    A perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal: the fraction turns over and the sign changes, and both moves are needed.

    m⊥=−135=−53,35⋅(−53)=−1m_{\perp} = -\frac{1}{\tfrac{3}{5}} = -\frac{5}{3}, \qquad \frac{3}{5} \cdot \left(-\frac{5}{3}\right) = -1m⊥​=−53​1​=−35​,53​⋅(−35​)=−1

    Doing only one of the two moves gives −35-\tfrac{3}{5}−53​ or 53\tfrac{5}{3}35​, whose products with 35\tfrac{3}{5}53​ are −925-\tfrac{9}{25}−259​ and 111.

  7. 7

    Which equation is the point-slope form of the line through (−2,−7)(-2, -7)(−2,−7) with slope 444?

    Answer choices for question 7

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Drops the minus sign on each coordinate, subtracting 777 and 222 instead of −7-7−7 and −2-2−2, so both signs come out wrong.

    You chose B: Subtracts the negative yyy-coordinate correctly but treats x1x_1x1​ as +2+2+2, so the parenthesis subtracts where it should add.

    You chose C: Subtracts the negative xxx-coordinate correctly but treats y1y_1y1​ as +7+7+7, so the left side subtracts where it should add.

    Point-slope form is built out of two subtractions, y−y1y - y_1y−y1​ and x−x1x - x_1x−x1​, and subtracting a negative coordinate turns into addition.

    y−(−7)=4(x−(−2)),y+7=4(x+2)y - (-7) = 4\bigl(x - (-2)\bigr), \qquad y + 7 = 4(x + 2)y−(−7)=4(x−(−2)),y+7=4(x+2)

    As a check, the point itself makes both sides zero: −7+7=0-7 + 7 = 0−7+7=0 and 4(−2+2)=04(-2 + 2) = 04(−2+2)=0.

  8. 8

    Line ggg passes through (−4,6)(-4, 6)(−4,6) and (9,6)(9, 6)(9,6). Line hhh passes through (5,−2)(5, -2)(5,−2) and (5,11)(5, 11)(5,11). What are their slopes?

    Answer choices for question 8

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Swaps the two cases, reading a repeated yyy-value as the upright line and a repeated xxx-value as the flat one.

    You chose C: Reports 130\tfrac{13}{0}013​ as 000, treating a zero denominator the way a zero numerator behaves.

    You chose D: Calls any slope built from a repeated coordinate undefined, without checking whether the repetition lands in the rise or in the run.

    Both points of ggg sit at the same height, so its rise is 000; both points of hhh sit in the same column, so its run is 000.

    mg=6−69−(−4)=013=0,mh=11−(−2)5−5=130m_g = \frac{6 - 6}{9 - (-4)} = \frac{0}{13} = 0, \qquad m_h = \frac{11 - (-2)}{5 - 5} = \frac{13}{0}mg​=9−(−4)6−6​=130​=0,mh​=5−511−(−2)​=013​

    A zero on top divides out to the number 000. A zero underneath divides out to nothing at all, so hhh has no slope: ggg is the horizontal line y=6y = 6y=6 and hhh is the vertical line x=5x = 5x=5.

  9. 9

    Rewritten in the form y=mx+by = mx + by=mx+b, what are the slope and the y-intercept of 6x+4y=106x + 4y = 106x+4y=10?

    Answer choices for question 9

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Reads both numbers off the standard-form equation without first solving for yyy.

    You chose B: Divides the xxx-term by 444 but leaves the constant on the right undivided.

    You chose D: Divides every term correctly but drops the minus sign that carrying 6x6x6x across the equals sign produced.

    Nothing on the page is the slope or the intercept until yyy stands alone, so carry the xxx-term across and divide every term by the coefficient of yyy.

    4y=−6x+10,y=−32x+524y = -6x + 10, \qquad y = -\tfrac{3}{2}x + \tfrac{5}{2}4y=−6x+10,y=−23​x+25​

    The slope is −32-\tfrac{3}{2}−23​ and the constant 52\tfrac{5}{2}25​ places the y-intercept at (0,52)\left(0, \tfrac{5}{2}\right)(0,25​). Setting x=0x = 0x=0 in the original equation gives 4y=104y = 104y=10 and confirms it.

  10. 10

    A diver ascends at a steady rate. Her depth ddd metres below the surface after ttt minutes of ascending is d=42−6td = 42 - 6td=42−6t. After how many minutes does she reach the surface?

    Answer choices for question 10

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Reports the constant term, which is the depth at t=0t = 0t=0, as though it answered a question about time.

    You chose C: Reports the 666 that multiplies ttt, the metres of depth lost each minute, instead of solving for d=0d = 0d=0.

    You chose D: Carries the 424242 across the equals sign without changing its sign, solving 6t=−426t = -426t=−42.

    Reaching the surface means the depth has fallen to zero, so this asks for the crossing where d=0d = 0d=0.

    0=42−6t,6t=42,t=70 = 42 - 6t, \qquad 6t = 42, \qquad t = 70=42−6t,6t=42,t=7

    Written as d=−6t+42d = -6t + 42d=−6t+42, the equation shows 424242 as the depth at the start and −6-6−6 as the change per minute; neither of those is the crossing itself.

    How are the lines y=27x+9y = \tfrac{2}{7}x + 9y=72​x+9 and 2x+7y=142x + 7y = 142x+7y=14 related?

    Answer choices for question 11

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Matches the two slopes by size alone and overlooks that one of them is negative.

    You chose B: Treats a change of sign as the perpendicular condition, though the fraction must turn over as well.

    You chose C: Sees 27\tfrac{2}{7}72​ in both and concludes they are one line, without noticing the difference in sign or comparing the constants 999 and 222.

    The second equation hides its slope until yyy stands alone.

    7y=−2x+14,y=−27x+27y = -2x + 14, \qquad y = -\tfrac{2}{7}x + 27y=−2x+14,y=−72​x+2

    The slopes are 27\tfrac{2}{7}72​ and −27-\tfrac{2}{7}−72​. They are not equal, so the lines are not parallel, and their product is 27⋅(−27)=−449\tfrac{2}{7} \cdot \left(-\tfrac{2}{7}\right) = -\tfrac{4}{49}72​⋅(−72​)=−494​, not −1-1−1, so they do not cross at a right angle either.

    A line passes through (−1,8)(-1, 8)(−1,8) and (3,−4)(3, -4)(3,−4). Which equation describes it?

    Answer choices for question 12

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Subtracts the yyy-values in one order and the xxx-values in the other, so the slope arrives as +3+3+3, and then fits the constant to (−1,8)(-1, 8)(−1,8).

    You chose C: Finds the slope correctly but takes the first point's yyy-coordinate as the constant, as though (−1,8)(-1, 8)(−1,8) sat on the yyy-axis.

    You chose D: Finds the slope correctly but solves −4=−9+b-4 = -9 + b−4=−9+b in the wrong direction, reporting b=−9−(−4)b = -9 - (-4)b=−9−(−4).

    Two points are not a point and a slope, so find the slope first, keeping both subtractions in the same order.

    m=−4−83−(−1)=−124=−3m = \frac{-4 - 8}{3 - (-1)} = \frac{-12}{4} = -3m=3−(−1)−4−8​=4−12​=−3

    Point-slope form with (3,−4)(3, -4)(3,−4) gives y+4=−3(x−3)y + 4 = -3(x - 3)y+4=−3(x−3), which tidies to y=−3x+5y = -3x + 5y=−3x+5. Both given points check: −3(−1)+5=8-3(-1) + 5 = 8−3(−1)+5=8 and −3(3)+5=−4-3(3) + 5 = -4−3(3)+5=−4.

    The graph of 2x+ky=122x + ky = 122x+ky=12 passes through (3,2)(3, 2)(3,2). What is its y-intercept?

    Answer choices for question 13

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Fixes k=2k = 2k=2 by matching it to the coefficient of xxx rather than by using the point that was given.

    You chose C: Finds kkk correctly but then sets y=0y = 0y=0, which locates the crossing of the other axis.

    You chose D: Reads the constant on the right as the height of the crossing, without dividing by the coefficient of yyy.

    The point lies on the graph, so its coordinates satisfy the equation, and that is what pins down kkk.

    2(3)+k(2)=12,2k=6,k=32(3) + k(2) = 12, \qquad 2k = 6, \qquad k = 32(3)+k(2)=12,2k=6,k=3

    The line is 2x+3y=122x + 3y = 122x+3y=12. Setting x=0x = 0x=0 gives 3y=123y = 123y=12, so the y-intercept is (0,4)(0, 4)(0,4).

    The points (−2,7)(-2, 7)(−2,7), (1,k)(1, k)(1,k) and (7,−5)(7, -5)(7,−5) all lie on one line. What is kkk?

    Answer choices for question 14

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Loses the minus sign on the slope, stepping 444 up from (−2,7)(-2, 7)(−2,7) instead of 444 down.

    You chose B: Takes the middle yyy-value to be halfway between the two outer ones, though x=1x = 1x=1 is not halfway between −2-2−2 and 777.

    You chose C: Works back from (7,−5)(7, -5)(7,−5) with the slope's sign dropped, falling a further 43\tfrac{4}{3}34​ per unit across the six units to x=1x = 1x=1.

    The two outer points fix the slope, and a line has only one slope, so the same value must hold over the shorter run as well.

    m=−5−77−(−2)=−129=−43m = \frac{-5 - 7}{7 - (-2)} = \frac{-12}{9} = -\frac{4}{3}m=7−(−2)−5−7​=9−12​=−34​

    The run from (−2,7)(-2, 7)(−2,7) to (1,k)(1, k)(1,k) is 333, so k−73=−43\dfrac{k - 7}{3} = -\dfrac{4}{3}3k−7​=−34​, giving k−7=−4k - 7 = -4k−7=−4 and k=3k = 3k=3. Checking the far side, the run from (1,3)(1, 3)(1,3) to (7,−5)(7, -5)(7,−5) is 666 and the rise is −8-8−8, again −43-\tfrac{4}{3}−34​.

  15. 15

    Which statement about the pair of lines y=−2y = -2y=−2 and x=7x = 7x=7 is correct?

    Answer choices for question 15

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Applies the product test to a pair in which one of the two lines has no slope number to multiply.

    You chose B: Reads "not slanted" as one shared direction, though one line is flat and the other stands upright.

    You chose D: Requires the slope test to certify every right angle, so a pair the test cannot reach is ruled out rather than settled another way.

    A flat line and an upright line cross square, so this pair is perpendicular. What is missing is a product to prove it with.

    my=−2=0,mx=7 is undefinedm_{y = -2} = 0, \qquad m_{x = 7} \text{ is undefined}my=−2​=0,mx=7​ is undefined

    There is no second number to multiply the 000 by, and −10-\tfrac{1}{0}−01​ is not a number either, so slope 000 has no negative reciprocal. The right angle here is settled by the two directions, one holding the height fixed and the other holding the column fixed, not by the slope test.

    Written as Ax+By=CAx + By = CAx+By=C with integer coefficients and A≥0A \ge 0A≥0, what does y−5=−34(x+8)y - 5 = -\tfrac{3}{4}(x + 8)y−5=−43​(x+8) become?

    Answer choices for question 16

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Distributes the −3-3−3 over the parenthesis as −3x+24-3x + 24−3x+24, flipping the sign of the second term.

    You chose C: Gathers the variable terms onto the side that leaves the leading coefficient negative, which the convention A≥0A \ge 0A≥0 rules out.

    You chose D: Carries the −20-20−20 to the right-hand side without changing its sign, so the two constants add rather than partly cancel.

    Clear the fraction by multiplying both sides by 444, distribute, then collect the variables on the left.

    4(y−5)=−3(x+8),4y−20=−3x−24,3x+4y=−44(y - 5) = -3(x + 8), \qquad 4y - 20 = -3x - 24, \qquad 3x + 4y = -44(y−5)=−3(x+8),4y−20=−3x−24,3x+4y=−4

    Adding 3x3x3x and 202020 to both sides leaves integer coefficients, a positive AAA, and no factor shared by 333, 444 and 444. As a check, the point (−8,5)(-8, 5)(−8,5) the equation was built on gives 3(−8)+4(5)=−43(-8) + 4(5) = -43(−8)+4(5)=−4.

    Answer choices for question 17

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Solves for ccc as −15-15−15 by dropping the minus sign on the yyy-term, then divides that by 888.

    You chose B: Divides the coefficient by the constant rather than the constant by the coefficient.

    You chose C: Uses the y-intercept's height −5-5−5 as the value of ccc, without solving −3y=c-3y = c−3y=c for it first.

    The given crossing is what setting x=0x = 0x=0 must return, and that pins down ccc.

    −3(−5)=c,c=15-3(-5) = c, \qquad c = 15−3(−5)=c,c=15

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Keeps the given line's own slope, which builds a line alongside it rather than one across it.

  20. 20

    The equation y−3=m(x+5)y - 3 = m(x + 5)y−3=m(x+5) describes a line for every value of mmm. Which point lies on that line no matter which mmm is chosen?

    Answer choices for question 20

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Reads the two numbers straight off the equation without reversing the signs that its subtractions impose.

    You chose B: Pairs the two constants in the order they are printed, taking the number beside yyy as the first coordinate.

    You chose D: Assumes the shared point must be the y-intercept, reading the 333 as the height at x=0x = 0x=0.

    Point-slope form is built so that its own point makes both sides zero, whatever multiplies the parenthesis.

    3−3=m(−5+5),0=m⋅0=03 - 3 = m(-5 + 5), \qquad 0 = m \cdot 0 = 03−3=m(−5+5),0=m⋅0=0

    This holds for every mmm, so (−5,3)(-5, 3)(−5,3) is on every line of the family. No other point can be: at any point with x≠−5x \ne -5x=−5 the equation y−3=m(x+5)y - 3 = m(x + 5)y−3=m(x+5) pins mmm to one value, so a different mmm moves the line off it.

    1. One number, read forwards and then backwards . 9 points. Question 1 of 10.

    9 pts

    A line is known by two of its points and by nothing else: (−6,11)(-6, 11)(−6,11) and (4,−9)(4, -9)(4,−9). Every part below is settled by that pair on its own.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Find the slope of the line, showing the substitution into the slope formula.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 3 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Find the point of the same line whose yyy-coordinate is −19-19−19.

      Carry your own answer forward Use whichever slope you produced in part A, even if it was not the expected one. The credit here is for treating the slope as the ratio of the known drop to the unknown run, and for moving in the direction that ratio demands, not for landing on a particular pair of numbers.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 3 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      In part A the slope came out of a change in xxx and a change in yyy; in part B it turned a known change in yyy back into a change in xxx. Say what your single number asserts about this line, in a sentence naming what happens to yyy when xxx increases by 111, and then say what part B shows about how far xxx must travel to bring yyy down by 101010.

      Carry your own answer forward Interpret whichever slope and whichever point you produced above, even if they were not the expected ones. The credit is for describing the slope as a rate that works in both directions, not for reproducing one particular pair of numbers.

      Explain what it means Words, not just symbols. Say what the number is telling you about the situation. 3 points

    The answer

    Part A

    m=−2m = -2m=−2.

    • −2-2−2 may be written −2010-\tfrac{20}{10}−1020​ before it is reduced; what is not the same is 222, which reverses the direction the line runs, or −12-\tfrac{1}{2}−21​, which divides the run by the rise

    Part B

    (9,−19)(9, -19)(9,−19).

    • (9,−19)(9, -19)(9,−19) only; an answer of (−1,−19)(-1, -19)(−1,−19) has moved to the left instead of the right, and (24,−19)(24, -19)(24,−19) has multiplied the drop by the slope instead of dividing by it

    Part C

    The slope −2-2−2 says that wherever you stand on the line, an increase of 111 in xxx is matched by a decrease of 222 in yyy. Part B shows that bringing yyy down by 101010 therefore takes an increase of 555 in xxx, because five steps of −2-2−2 make −10-10−10.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The rise is the difference of the yyy-values and the run is the difference of the xxx-values, taken in the same order.

    m=−9−114−(−6)=−2010=−2.m = \frac{-9 - 11}{4 - (-6)} = \frac{-20}{10} = -2.m=4−(−6)−9−11​=10−20​=−2.

    The value is negative, so the line falls as it moves to the right.

    Part B

    Nothing here needs the line's equation. The drop from (4,−9)(4, -9)(4,−9) down to a height of −19-19−19 is −10-10−10, and the slope fixes the ratio of that drop to the run it takes.

    −19−(−9)x−4=−2,−10x−4=−2,x−4=5,x=9.\frac{-19 - (-9)}{x - 4} = -2, \qquad \frac{-10}{x - 4} = -2, \qquad x - 4 = 5, \qquad x = 9.x−4−19−(−9)​=−2,x−4−10​=−2,x−4=5,x=9.

    The point is (9,−19)(9, -19)(9,−19). Checking against the other given point, the run from (−6,11)(-6, 11)(−6,11) to (9,−19)(9, -19)(9,−19) is 151515 and the rise is −30-30−30, again a slope of −2-2−2.

    Part C

    A slope is a rate, not a single journey. The value −2-2−2 is what one unit of run buys in rise:

    run 1  ⟶  rise −2.\text{run } 1 \;\longrightarrow\; \text{rise } -2.run 1⟶rise −2.

    That is why it can be used in either direction. Reading it forwards turns a run into a rise. Reading it backwards turns a rise into a run, which is what part B did: a required rise of −10-10−10 is five copies of −2-2−2, so it takes five copies of the matching run, an increase of 555 in xxx.

    In one line

    The slope is m=−2m = -2m=−2, and the point of the line whose yyy-coordinate is −19-19−19 is (9,−19)(9, -19)(9,−19). The slope says that yyy falls by 222 for every 111 that xxx rises, everywhere along the line, which is exactly why a required fall of 101010 in yyy costs a run of 555 in xxx.

    2. Two crossings a grid cannot hold . 13 points. Question 2 of 10.

    13 pts

    The intercept method draws a line from exactly two of its solutions, the two places where it meets the axes. This question runs it on two equations and then asks what becomes of the drawing when those two places do not sit on grid corners.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Find both intercepts of 9x−4y=369x - 4y = 369x−4y=36. Report each as an ordered pair, and name the variable you zeroed to reach it.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 3 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Now find both intercepts of 5x+6y=45x + 6y = 45x+6y=4. Then find one further solution of 5x+6y=45x + 6y = 45x+6y=4 whose two coordinates are both integers.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 5 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Part B produced one solution of 5x+6y=45x + 6y = 45x+6y=4 that sits exactly on a grid corner. Find a second one, state the step across and the step up or down that carries any such solution to the next, and show why a step of that size leaves the equation satisfied. Then say what fixes each of the two crossings where it is, and why no way of drawing the line brings either of them onto a corner.

      Carry your own answer forward Step off from whichever grid-corner solution you produced in part B, and speak about whichever crossings you computed there, even if they were not the expected ones. The credit is for a step that keeps the equation satisfied and for showing why it does, not for a particular pair of numbers.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    The x-intercept is (4,0)(4, 0)(4,0), obtained by setting y=0y = 0y=0; the y-intercept is (0,−9)(0, -9)(0,−9), obtained by setting x=0x = 0x=0.

    • (4,0)(4, 0)(4,0) and (0,−9)(0, -9)(0,−9); the pair (0,4)(0, 4)(0,4) and (−9,0)(-9, 0)(−9,0) is the same arithmetic with the coordinates in the wrong slots, and (9,0)(9, 0)(9,0) has divided 363636 by 444, the coefficient of the term just zeroed out

    Part B

    The intercepts are (45,0)\left(\tfrac{4}{5}, 0\right)(54​,0) and (0,23)\left(0, \tfrac{2}{3}\right)(0,32​). One solution with integer coordinates is (2,−1)(2, -1)(2,−1).

    • any pair of integers satisfying the equation is acceptable for the third point, for instance (−4,4)(-4, 4)(−4,4) or (8,−6)(8, -6)(8,−6); what is not acceptable is a pair that has been rounded rather than solved

    Part C

    Stepping 666 across and 555 down carries (2,−1)(2, -1)(2,−1) to (8,−6)(8, -6)(8,−6); the step leaves the left side at 444, because 5(6)+6(−5)=05(6) + 6(-5) = 05(6)+6(−5)=0. The crossings cannot be moved: the line meets each axis exactly once, at the values part B computed, 45\tfrac{4}{5}54​ and 23\tfrac{2}{3}32​, and neither is an integer.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Each axis is the set of points whose other coordinate is zero, so zero the coordinate belonging to the axis you are crossing.

    9x−4(0)=36  ⟹  x=4,9(0)−4y=36  ⟹  y=−9.9x - 4(0) = 36 \implies x = 4, \qquad 9(0) - 4y = 36 \implies y = -9.9x−4(0)=36⟹x=4,9(0)−4y=36⟹y=−9.

    So the graph crosses the x-axis at (4,0)(4, 0)(4,0) and the y-axis at (0,−9)(0, -9)(0,−9).

    Part B

    The two crossings come from the same two substitutions as before, and this time neither lands on an integer.

    5x=4  ⟹  x=45,6y=4  ⟹  y=23.5x = 4 \implies x = \tfrac{4}{5}, \qquad 6y = 4 \implies y = \tfrac{2}{3}.5x=4⟹x=54​,6y=4⟹y=32​.

    For a solution with integer coordinates, choose an xxx that leaves a multiple of 666 behind. Taking x=2x = 2x=2 gives 10+6y=410 + 6y = 410+6y=4, so 6y=−66y = -66y=−6 and y=−1y = -1y=−1:

    5(2)+6(−1)=10−6=4.5(2) + 6(-1) = 10 - 6 = 4.5(2)+6(−1)=10−6=4.

    So (2,−1)(2, -1)(2,−1) is on the line and sits exactly on a grid corner.

    Part C

    A step that carries one solution to another is one whose two changes cancel on the left. Adding 666 to xxx adds 303030 to 5x5x5x, and taking 555 off yyy takes 303030 off 6y6y6y.

    5(x+6)+6(y−5)=5x+6y+30−30=5x+6y5(x + 6) + 6(y - 5) = 5x + 6y + 30 - 30 = 5x + 6y5(x+6)+6(y−5)=5x+6y+30−30=5x+6y

    So the left side is left exactly as it was, and any solution steps to another. From (2,−1)(2, -1)(2,−1) the step reaches (8,−6)(8, -6)(8,−6), and 5(8)+6(−6)=40−36=45(8) + 6(-6) = 40 - 36 = 45(8)+6(−6)=40−36=4 confirms it; taken backwards it reaches (−4,4)(-4, 4)(−4,4), and 5(−4)+6(4)=45(-4) + 6(4) = 45(−4)+6(4)=4 as well. Repeating it in either direction supplies grid corners as far out as the drawing needs.

    The crossings admit no such treatment. This line is neither horizontal nor vertical, so it meets each axis exactly once, and part B computed those two points exactly: x=45x = \tfrac{4}{5}x=54​ when y=0y = 0y=0, and y=23y = \tfrac{2}{3}y=32​ when x=0x = 0x=0. Those are results rather than choices, so nothing about how the line is drawn or how far it is extended puts either crossing on a corner. The line is still drawn exactly; it is just drawn through corners the equation supplies instead.

    In one line

    The graph of 9x−4y=369x - 4y = 369x−4y=36 crosses the axes at (4,0)(4, 0)(4,0), from y=0y = 0y=0, and at (0,−9)(0, -9)(0,−9), from x=0x = 0x=0. The graph of 5x+6y=45x + 6y = 45x+6y=4 crosses at (45,0)\left(\tfrac{4}{5}, 0\right)(54​,0) and (0,23)\left(0, \tfrac{2}{3}\right)(0,32​), and (2,−1)(2, -1)(2,−1) is a solution whose coordinates are both integers. Stepping 666 across and 555 down from it reaches another, (8,−6)(8, -6)(8,−6), because 5(6)+6(−5)=05(6) + 6(-5) = 05(6)+6(−5)=0 leaves the left side untouched. The two crossings cannot be brought onto corners at all: the line meets each axis exactly once, and those single points are 45\tfrac{4}{5}54​ and 23\tfrac{2}{3}32​.

    12 pts

    Two candles are lit at the same moment, and each burns down at its own steady rate. Candle A's height in centimetres after ttt hours is given by h=24−4th = 24 - 4th=24−4t. Candle B's height satisfies 2t+h=152t + h = 152t+h=15.

Say which candle is the taller at each of those two moments, and then say what the pair of answers shows about calling one of the two candles the taller one. Name the number in each equation that decides which candle is eventually the taller.

      Carry your own answer forward Use whichever equations you produced above, even if they were not the expected ones. The credit here is for evaluating both models at both times, for reading the comparison honestly, and for naming which of the two numbers in each equation controls the long run.

      Explain what it means Words, not just symbols. Say what the number is telling you about the situation. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    The slope is −4-4−4 and the hhh-intercept is (0,24)(0, 24)(0,24): candle A stands 242424 cm tall when it is lit and loses 444 cm of height every hour.

    • the intercept may be given as the number 242424 rather than the point (0,24)(0, 24)(0,24), provided the units are said; what is not the same is a slope of 242424, which reads the constant term as the rate

    Part B

    h=−2t+15h = -2t + 15h=−2t+15, so candle B's slope is −2-2−2 and its hhh-intercept is (0,15)(0, 15)(0,15).

    • h=15−2th = 15 - 2th=15−2t is the same equation with the terms in the other order; what is not the same is a slope of 222, which has lost the sign that carrying 2t2t2t across produced

    Part C

    At t=0t = 0t=0 candle A is taller, 242424 cm against 151515 cm. At t=5t = 5t=5 candle B is taller, 555 cm against 444 cm. So neither is the taller candle outright: the order swaps. The slopes decide the eventual order, since A loses height at twice B's rate and must fall below it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The equation lists its terms out of order, so put them in the order the form expects before reading anything off.

    h=24−4t=−4t+24.h = 24 - 4t = -4t + 24.h=24−4t=−4t+24.

    The number multiplying ttt is −4-4−4, so the slope is −4-4−4 centimetres per hour, a loss. The constant is 242424, so the hhh-intercept is (0,24)(0, 24)(0,24), the height at the moment of lighting.

    Part B

    Nothing on the page is the slope or the intercept until hhh is alone, so carry the ttt-term across.

    2t+h=15,h=−2t+15.2t + h = 15, \qquad h = -2t + 15.2t+h=15,h=−2t+15.

    The slope is −2-2−2 centimetres per hour and the hhh-intercept is (0,15)(0, 15)(0,15). Setting t=0t = 0t=0 in the original equation gives h=15h = 15h=15 and confirms it.

    Part C

    Evaluate both equations at both times.

    At t=0:hA=24,hB=15.At t=5:hA=24−20=4,hB=15−10=5.\text{At } t = 0: \quad h_A = 24, \quad h_B = 15. \qquad \text{At } t = 5: \quad h_A = 24 - 20 = 4, \quad h_B = 15 - 10 = 5.At t=0:hA​=24,hB​=15.At t=5:hA​=24−20=4,hB​=15−10=5.

    Candle A starts ahead and finishes behind, so "the taller candle" is not a property either one has. It is a comparison that depends on when it is made. What settles the eventual order is the pair of slopes: A loses 444 cm an hour against B's 222 cm an hour, so the gap of 999 cm that A begins with is eaten away at 222 cm an hour and cannot last. The intercepts say only where the two start.

    In one line

    Candle A has slope −4-4−4 and hhh-intercept (0,24)(0, 24)(0,24): it is 242424 cm tall when lit and loses 444 cm an hour. Candle B's equation is h=−2t+15h = -2t + 15h=−2t+15, with slope −2-2−2 and hhh-intercept (0,15)(0, 15)(0,15). At t=0t = 0t=0 candle A is taller, 242424 cm against 151515 cm, and at t=5t = 5t=5 candle B is taller, 555 cm against 444 cm, so neither is the taller candle outright. The slopes settle the eventual order, because A loses height at twice B's rate.

    • the unsimplified y−1=−23(x−4)y - 1 = -\tfrac{2}{3}(x - 4)y−1=−32​(x−4) is the same line; what is not the same is a slope of 32\tfrac{3}{2}23​ or of −32-\tfrac{3}{2}−23​, neither of which multiplies with 32\tfrac{3}{2}23​ to give −1-1−1

    There is no such line. The only line through TTT with KKK's slope is y=32x−5y = \tfrac{3}{2}x - 5y=23​x−5, which is KKK itself, since its slope and its constant both match KKK's. A line cannot fail to meet itself, so nothing through TTT avoids KKK.

    Part C

    The right-angle line meets KKK at exactly one point, TTT itself. The line built with KKK's slope is KKK, so it shares every point of KKK.     Part A

    The slope of KKK is 32\tfrac{3}{2}23​, so a line crossing it at a right angle has the negative reciprocal slope, the fraction turned over and the sign changed.

    m⊥=−23,32⋅(−23)=−1.m_{\perp} = -\frac{2}{3}, \qquad \frac{3}{2} \cdot \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) = -1.m⊥​=−32​,23​⋅(−32​)=−1.

    Part B

    A line that never meets KKK must have KKK's slope, 32\tfrac{3}{2}23​, since two lines whose slopes differ cross exactly once. So build the line through TTT with that slope:

    y−1=32(x−4),y=32x−5.y - 1 = \tfrac{3}{2}(x - 4), \qquad y = \tfrac{3}{2}x - 5.y−1=23​(x−4),y=23​x−5.

Equal slopes alone would only have made the two lines parallel; here the constants are equal as well, −5-5−5 and −5-5−5, and equal slope together with equal constant is one line written twice. The reason is visible in TTT itself: substituting x=4x = 4x=4 into KKK gives 32(4)−5=1\tfrac{3}{2}(4) - 5 = 123​(4)−5=1, so TTT was on KKK all along, and every line through a point of KKK meets KKK at least there.

    Part C

    Two lines with different slopes cross exactly once, so the right-angle line meets KKK at a single point, and since it was built through TTT and TTT lies on KKK, that point is TTT.

    The second line was not a different line at all, so the count is not one but every point of KKK.

    Moving the point off KKK changes the second case completely. With T=(4,2)T = (4, 2)T=(4,2), note first that 32(4)−5=1≠2\tfrac{3}{2}(4) - 5 = 1 \ne 223​(4)−5=1=2, so the point is off KKK, and the line through it with KKK's slope is

    Equal slopes, constants −4-4−4 and −5-5−5 that differ, so this really is parallel: a second line that never meets KKK, sharing no point at all. Whether the request in part B can be met turns entirely on whether the given point lies on KKK.

There is no line through TTT that never meets KKK: the only line through TTT with KKK's slope has KKK's constant too, so it is KKK itself.     Part A

    (3,−4)(3, -4)(3,−4) is the common point, each equation fixing one coordinate. It lies on all three graphs, (−2,−4)(-2, -4)(−2,−4) on y=−4y = -4y=−4 alone, and (3,8)(3, 8)(3,8) on x=3x = 3x=3 alone.

    On 2x−5y=262x - 5y = 262x−5y=26 they are (28,6)(28, 6)(28,6) and (−7,−8)(-7, -8)(−7,−8). On y=−4y = -4y=−4 no point has height 666, that graph holding only the height −4-4−4, while (−7,−4)(-7, -4)(−7,−4) is its one point in that column.

So a missing yyy is decided, a missing xxx is unconstrained and every number works, and a point whose stated yyy is not −4-4−4 can be rescued by no xxx.     Worked solution

    Part A

    An equation naming one letter is satisfied when that letter matches, whatever the other one is, so the two one-letter graphs make one demand each: y=−4y = -4y=−4 fixes the height and x=3x = 3x=3 fixes the column, and (3,−4)(3, -4)(3,−4) is the only pair meeting both. The third equation is different in kind, since it has to be satisfied by the pair together.

    2(3)−5(−4)=6+20=26,2(−2)−5(−4)=−4+20=16,2(3)−5(8)=6−40=−34.2(3) - 5(-4) = 6 + 20 = 26, \qquad 2(-2) - 5(-4) = -4 + 20 = 16, \qquad 2(3) - 5(8) = 6 - 40 = -34.2(3)−5(−4)=6+20=26,2(−2)−5(−4)=−4+20=16,2(3)−5(8)=6−40=−34.

    So (3,−4)(3, -4)(3,−4) satisfies 2x−5y=262x - 5y = 262x−5y=26 as well, putting it on all three graphs. The point (−2,−4)(-2, -4)(−2,−4) has the right height but the wrong column and returns 161616, so it lies on y=−4y = -4y=−4 alone. The point (3,8)(3, 8)(3,8) has the right column but the wrong height and returns −34-34−34, so it lies on x=3x = 3x=3 alone.

    Part B

    On 2x−5y=262x - 5y = 262x−5y=26 each search leaves one unknown coordinate and is solved by substitution.

    2x−5(6)=26  ⟹  2x=56  ⟹  x=28,2(−7)−5y=26  ⟹  −5y=40  ⟹  y=−8.2x - 5(6) = 26 \implies 2x = 56 \implies x = 28, \qquad 2(-7) - 5y = 26 \implies -5y = 40 \implies y = -8.2x−5(6)=26⟹2x=56⟹x=28,2(−7)−5y=26⟹−5y=40⟹y=−8.

    So the two points are (28,6)(28, 6)(28,6) and (−7,−8)(-7, -8)(−7,−8). On y=−4y = -4y=−4 the two searches behave quite differently. A point of height 666 would need

    6=−46 = -46=−4

    to hold, since the graph holds every point of height −4-4−4 and no other, and no first coordinate can rescue it. A point with first coordinate −7-7−7 instead has its height unknown, and the equation names it outright, so the point is (−7,−4)(-7, -4)(−7,−4) and there is no other.

    Part C

    Read y=−4y = -4y=−4 as the pair of demands it actually makes. It demands that the height be −4-4−4, and it demands nothing whatever of the column, which is the same as writing it 0⋅x+y=−40 \cdot x + y = -40⋅x+y=−4: the coefficient of xxx is zero, so no value of xxx can affect whether the equation holds.

    0⋅x+y=−4.0 \cdot x + y = -4.0⋅x+y=−4.

    Three behaviours follow directly. If the height is unknown, the equation names it, and the search returns exactly one value. If the height is given as −4-4−4 and the column is unknown, the equation is already satisfied and every column works, so the search returns every number. If the height is given as anything else, no column can help, and the search returns nothing.

    On the graph, the second case is the whole horizontal line, a single height stretching across every column, and the third case is a point sitting off that line, at the wrong height. The same account runs for x=3x = 3x=3 with the roles of the two letters exchanged, which is why it is a vertical line.

On y=−4y = -4y=−4 no point has height 666, since that height is already wrong, while (−7,−4)(-7, -4)(−7,−4) is the one point in that column. An equation naming only one letter pins that letter and leaves the other entirely free, which is why one search is determined, one is impossible, and one would return every point of the line at once: the graph is a single height carrying every column.

The slopes identify each relationship; the unequal constants complete the parallel verdict.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Neither equation shows its slope, so solve each for yyy first.

    4x−5y=30  ⟹  y=45x−6,ax+8y=5  ⟹  y=−a8x+58.4x - 5y = 30 \implies y = \tfrac{4}{5}x - 6, \qquad ax + 8y = 5 \implies y = -\tfrac{a}{8}x + \tfrac{5}{8}.4x−5y=30⟹y=54​x−6,ax+8y=5⟹y=−8a​x+85​.

    A right-angle crossing needs the second slope to be the negative reciprocal of 45\tfrac{4}{5}54​, which is −54-\tfrac{5}{4}−45​:

    −a8=−54,a=10.-\frac{a}{8} = -\frac{5}{4}, \qquad a = 10.−8a​=−45​,a=10.

    Checking, 45⋅(−54)=−1\tfrac{4}{5} \cdot \left(-\tfrac{5}{4}\right) = -154​⋅(−45​)=−1.

    Part B

    With a=10a = 10a=10 the second equation is 10x+8y=510x + 8y = 510x+8y=5, and solving for yyy divides every term by 888:

    8y=−10x+5,y=−54x+58.8y = -10x + 5, \qquad y = -\tfrac{5}{4}x + \tfrac{5}{8}.8y=−10x+5,y=−45​x+85​.

    A line that never meets L1L_1L1​ must carry L1L_1L1​'s slope, 45\tfrac{4}{5}54​, since two lines with different slopes cross exactly once. Through the origin, the constant is 000:

    y−0=45(x−0),y=45x.y - 0 = \tfrac{4}{5}(x - 0), \qquad y = \tfrac{4}{5}x.y−0=54​(x−0),y=54​x.

    Its constant 000 differs from L1L_1L1​'s −6-6−6, so L3L_3L3​ really is a second line and not L1L_1L1​ written again, and two distinct lines of equal slope never meet.

    Part C

    The three slopes are 45\tfrac{4}{5}54​, −54-\tfrac{5}{4}−45​ and 45\tfrac{4}{5}54​, with constants −6-6−6, 58\tfrac{5}{8}85​ and 000.

    45⋅(−54)=−1,(−54)⋅45=−1,45=45.\tfrac{4}{5} \cdot \left(-\tfrac{5}{4}\right) = -1, \qquad \left(-\tfrac{5}{4}\right) \cdot \tfrac{4}{5} = -1, \qquad \tfrac{4}{5} = \tfrac{4}{5}.54​⋅(−45​)=−1,(−45​)⋅54​=−1,54​=54​.

    Each of the first two products is −1-1−1, which settles those two pairs as perpendicular on the slopes alone. The third comparison is not yet a verdict. Equal slopes leave two possibilities open, two parallel lines or one line written twice, and only the constants separate them: −6-6−6 and 000 are different, so L1L_1L1​ and L3L_3L3​ are two lines, and two distinct lines of equal slope are parallel.

    So the slopes carry the work in all three pairs and finish it in the two perpendicular ones. The parallel verdict is the one that needs both numbers, the equal slopes to name the relationship and the unequal constants to establish that there are two lines to be in it.

    In one line

    a=10a = 10a=10, so L2L_2L2​ is 10x+8y=510x + 8y = 510x+8y=5, that is y=−54x+58y = -\tfrac{5}{4}x + \tfrac{5}{8}y=−45​x+85​, and L3L_3L3​ is y=45xy = \tfrac{4}{5}xy=54​x. Of the three pairs, L1L_1L1​ with L2L_2L2​ and L2L_2L2​ with L3L_3L3​ are perpendicular, each product of slopes being −1-1−1, while L1L_1L1​ and L3L_3L3​ share the slope 45\tfrac{4}{5}54​ and carry the different constants −6-6−6 and 000, which makes them parallel. The slopes identify every relationship here, and the constants are what turn equal slopes into a parallel verdict rather than one line written twice.

    9. A form with three rules attached to it . 14 points. Question 9 of 10.

    14 pts

    Standard form asks for more than a rearrangement. It asks for Ax+By=CAx + By = CAx+By=C with AAA, BBB and CCC integers, with AAA zero or positive, and with the three sharing no common factor. Two lines are written that way below, and then a further request is made of one of them.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Write the equation of the line through (2,−9)(2, -9)(2,−9) with slope 73\tfrac{7}{3}37​, first in point-slope form and then in standard form under the three conditions above.

    2. B
      Part B.

    3. C
      Part C.

      Your part A line is now wanted with 666 as the coefficient of yyy. Decide whether that can be produced without breaking any of the three conditions in the stem, and justify the verdict by naming exactly which rescaling would be required and saying what it does to the equation.

The credit is for identifying the single multiplier that could do the job and for checking it against each condition in turn.

    The answer

    Part A

    y+9=73(x−2)y + 9 = \tfrac{7}{3}(x - 2)y+9=37​(x−2) in point-slope form, and 7x−3y=417x - 3y = 417x−3y=41 in standard form.

    • −7x+3y=−41-7x + 3y = -41−7x+3y=−41 is the same line but leaves the leading coefficient negative, which the conditions rule out; 14x−6y=8214x - 6y = 8214x−6y=82 is also the same line but its three numbers share the factor 222

    Part B

    3x+7y=−573x + 7y = -573x+7y=−57.

    • −3x−7y=57-3x - 7y = 57−3x−7y=57 is the same line with a negative leading coefficient, which the conditions rule out; 3x+7y=573x + 7y = 573x+7y=57 has lost a sign in the arithmetic and is a different line

    Part C

    It cannot. The only rescaling that turns the coefficient −3-3−3 into 666 is multiplication by −2-2−2, which gives −14x+6y=−82-14x + 6y = -82−14x+6y=−82. That leaves the leading coefficient negative and gives all three numbers the common factor 222, so it breaks two of the three conditions at once.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Point-slope form takes the point and the slope with the signs its subtractions impose, so y−(−9)y - (-9)y−(−9) becomes y+9y + 9y+9.

    y+9=73(x−2).y + 9 = \tfrac{7}{3}(x - 2).y+9=37​(x−2).

    Clear the fraction by multiplying both sides by 333, then distribute and collect.

    3(y+9)=7(x−2),3y+27=7x−14,7x−3y=41.3(y + 9) = 7(x - 2), \qquad 3y + 27 = 7x - 14, \qquad 7x - 3y = 41.3(y+9)=7(x−2),3y+27=7x−14,7x−3y=41.

    The coefficients are integers, A=7A = 7A=7 is positive, and 777, 333 and 414141 share no factor. Substituting (2,−9)(2, -9)(2,−9) gives 14+27=4114 + 27 = 4114+27=41, so the point is on it.

    Part B

    Point-slope form again, then clear the denominator 777.

    y+9=−37(x−2),7(y+9)=−3(x−2),7y+63=−3x+6.y + 9 = -\tfrac{3}{7}(x - 2), \qquad 7(y + 9) = -3(x - 2), \qquad 7y + 63 = -3x + 6.y+9=−73​(x−2),7(y+9)=−3(x−2),7y+63=−3x+6.

    Collect the variables on the left and the constants on the right:

    3x+7y=−57.3x + 7y = -57.3x+7y=−57.

    The coefficients are integers, A=3A = 3A=3 is positive, and 333, 777 and 575757 share no factor, since 57=3×1957 = 3 \times 1957=3×19 but 777 is prime to both. Substituting (2,−9)(2, -9)(2,−9) gives 6−63=−576 - 63 = -576−63=−57.

    Part C

    Multiplying an equation through by a nonzero number never changes which pairs satisfy it, so the request is only about how the line is written, not about which line it is. The coefficient of yyy in 7x−3y=417x - 3y = 417x−3y=41 is −3-3−3, and the multiplier that sends −3-3−3 to 666 is settled:

    −3k=6  ⟹  k=−2.-3k = 6 \implies k = -2.−3k=6⟹k=−2.

    No other multiplier will do, so there is exactly one candidate to inspect.

    −2(7x−3y)=−2(41),−14x+6y=−82.-2(7x - 3y) = -2(41), \qquad -14x + 6y = -82.−2(7x−3y)=−2(41),−14x+6y=−82.

    Now test it against the conditions. The coefficients are integers, which is fine. But A=−14A = -14A=−14 is negative, and the convention asks for AAA zero or positive. And −14-14−14, 666 and −82-82−82 are all even, so the three share the factor 222, which the last condition also forbids. Both failures come from the same source: a negative multiplier flips the sign of AAA, and an even multiplier makes every coefficient even, and −2-2−2 is both. So the request cannot be met, and the honest answer is to say which condition would have to be waived.

    In one line

    The first line is y+9=73(x−2)y + 9 = \tfrac{7}{3}(x - 2)y+9=37​(x−2) in point-slope form and 7x−3y=417x - 3y = 417x−3y=41 in standard form. The second is 3x+7y=−573x + 7y = -573x+7y=−57. The first cannot be written with 666 as the coefficient of yyy under these conditions: the only multiplier that produces it is −2-2−2, giving −14x+6y=−82-14x + 6y = -82−14x+6y=−82, which leaves the leading coefficient negative and gives the three numbers the common factor 222.

    10. A shortcut for reading a slope off standard form . 17 points. Question 10 of 10.

    17 pts

    A shortcut is sometimes used to read a slope out of an equation written as Ax+By=CAx + By = CAx+By=C: take the coefficient of xxx over the coefficient of yyy, with the signs exactly as they stand on the page, and call that the slope. Below it is applied to two lines, and the two numbers it returns are multiplied together. Both equations here have a nonzero coefficient on yyy. The two lines are 6x−15y=456x - 15y = 456x−15y=45 and 10x+4y=910x + 4y = 910x+4y=9.

    1. A
      Part A.

The credit here is for applying the product test twice and reporting both outcomes honestly.

    3. C
      Part C.

      Set your two pairs of numbers from part A beside your two verdicts from part B, and say exactly what the shortcut does wrong. Then decide how far it can be trusted, keeping throughout to equations whose coefficient on yyy is not zero: name the questions about a PAIR of lines that it will always answer correctly and say why, and then say for which single lines it reports the slope wrongly and for which it happens to report it correctly.

      Carry your own answer forward Argue from whatever pattern your own numbers in part A showed, even if it was not the expected one, and say honestly what it does and does not license. The credit is for naming the omitted step, for showing why a comparison of two slopes survives it, and for identifying which lines the error does not touch.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 7 points

    The answer

    Part A

    The true slopes are 25\tfrac{2}{5}52​ and −52-\tfrac{5}{2}−25​. The shortcut returns −25-\tfrac{2}{5}−52​ and 52\tfrac{5}{2}25​.

    • the shortcut's values may be left unreduced as 6−15\tfrac{6}{-15}−156​ and 104\tfrac{10}{4}410​; what is not acceptable is reporting the shortcut's value as the true slope of either line

    Part B

    They do cross at a right angle, since 25⋅(−52)=−1\tfrac{2}{5} \cdot \left(-\tfrac{5}{2}\right) = -152​⋅(−25​)=−1. The shortcut would have reached the same decision, because its two numbers also multiply to −1-1−1: (−25)⋅52=−1\left(-\tfrac{2}{5}\right) \cdot \tfrac{5}{2} = -1(−52​)⋅25​=−1. A wrong pair of slopes has produced the right verdict.

    Part C

    It drops the sign change that carrying the xxx-term across produces, so it returns the opposite of the true slope. Negating both slopes leaves both pair tests untouched, so pair verdicts survive it. A tilting line's slope comes out with the wrong sign; a horizontal line's 000 is its own opposite and escapes.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Solve each equation for yyy, dividing every term by the coefficient of yyy and watching what happens when that coefficient is negative.

    −15y=−6x+45  ⟹  y=25x−3,4y=−10x+9  ⟹  y=−52x+94.-15y = -6x + 45 \implies y = \tfrac{2}{5}x - 3, \qquad 4y = -10x + 9 \implies y = -\tfrac{5}{2}x + \tfrac{9}{4}.−15y=−6x+45⟹y=52​x−3,4y=−10x+9⟹y=−25​x+49​.

    So the true slopes are 25\tfrac{2}{5}52​ and −52-\tfrac{5}{2}−25​. The shortcut instead reads the coefficients straight off the page:

    6−15=−25,104=52.\frac{6}{-15} = -\frac{2}{5}, \qquad \frac{10}{4} = \frac{5}{2}.−156​=−52​,410​=25​.

    Each of the shortcut's numbers is the opposite of the corresponding true slope.

    Part B

    Apply the product test to the true slopes first.

    25⋅(−52)=−1010=−1.\frac{2}{5} \cdot \left(-\frac{5}{2}\right) = -\frac{10}{10} = -1.52​⋅(−25​)=−1010​=−1.

    The product is −1-1−1, so the two lines do meet at a right angle. Now apply the same test to what the shortcut returned.

    (−25)⋅52=−1010=−1.\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right) \cdot \frac{5}{2} = -\frac{10}{10} = -1.(−52​)⋅25​=−1010​=−1.

    The same verdict, from two numbers neither of which is a slope of either line. Nothing has been corrected along the way; the wrong pair simply happens to carry the same product.

    Part C

    What it does wrong. Solving Ax+By=CAx + By = CAx+By=C for yyy begins by moving the xxx-term to the other side, and moving it changes its sign. The shortcut skips that move and reads the coefficient where it stands, so it returns the opposite of the true slope every time.

    shortcut=AB,truth=−AB.\text{shortcut} = \frac{A}{B}, \qquad \text{truth} = -\frac{A}{B}.shortcut=BA​,truth=−BA​.

    Why the pair questions survive. Both of the chapter's tests compare two slopes, and negating both leaves both comparisons alone. For the right-angle test, the two minus signs cancel in the product:

    (−m1)(−m2)=m1m2.(-m_1)(-m_2) = m_1 m_2.(−m1​)(−m2​)=m1​m2​.

    So the shortcut's product is the true product, and it returns −1-1−1 exactly when the truth does. For the parallel test, negating both sides of an equality keeps it true and negating back restores it, so −m1=−m2-m_1 = -m_2−m1​=−m2​ holds precisely when m1=m2m_1 = m_2m1​=m2​. Both verdicts therefore come out right, for any two equations carrying a nonzero coefficient on yyy, however wrong the two inputs are.

    Where it fails. Every question about one line on its own goes wrong: the slope itself, whether the line rises or falls as xxx increases, the negative reciprocal built from it, and any equation written using it. Among these equations there is exactly one escape. The shortcut and the truth agree when AB=−AB\tfrac{A}{B} = -\tfrac{A}{B}BA​=−BA​, which forces A=0A = 0A=0, and A=0A = 0A=0 is a horizontal line. So a horizontal line's slope of 000 is reported correctly, because 000 is its own opposite, and every line that actually tilts is reported with the wrong sign.

    The case held back. All of that assumed a nonzero coefficient on yyy, which is what makes AB\tfrac{A}{B}BA​ a number at all. If B=0B = 0B=0 the equation reads Ax=CAx = CAx=C, a vertical line: the shortcut asks for A0\tfrac{A}{0}0A​ and returns nothing, and the true slope is undefined as well, so there is no number here to report rightly or wrongly. A pair containing such a line falls outside the product test for the same reason, one of the two numbers it needs not existing, and is settled by the two directions instead.

    In one line

    The true slopes are 25\tfrac{2}{5}52​ and −52-\tfrac{5}{2}−25​, while the shortcut returns −25-\tfrac{2}{5}−52​ and 52\tfrac{5}{2}25​. Both pairs multiply to −1-1−1, so the lines do cross at a right angle and the shortcut reaches that verdict too. The shortcut omits the sign change that carrying the xxx-term across produces, so it returns the opposite of the true slope. Negating both slopes leaves the product test and the equal-slopes test untouched, so for equations whose coefficient on yyy is not zero its verdicts about a pair are always right; among those lines the slope of any tilting one comes out with the wrong sign, and only a horizontal line escapes, because 000 is its own opposite. A zero coefficient on yyy sits outside all of it: that equation is a vertical line, where the shortcut returns nothing and there is no slope to compare.

  • Isolates the yyy-term and then divides every term on both sides by its coefficient, leaving yyy with a coefficient of 111. 2
  • Reads the slope off the rearranged form and states whether it agrees with the counted one. 2

Part C 5

  • Explains that fixing the slope leaves one unknown constant, and that requiring a known point determines it uniquely. 3
  • Substitutes one marked corner into the slope-intercept form and solves for the constant, showing the arithmetic. 2

8. Three lines built around one 15 points

Part A 5

  • Solves both equations for yyy before treating any coefficient as a slope. 2
  • Sets the second slope equal to the negative reciprocal of the first, turning the fraction over and changing the sign. 2
  • Reports a single value for aaa and confirms the product of the two slopes. 1

Part B 5

  • Divides every term by the coefficient of yyy, so that yyy ends with a coefficient of 111. 2
  • Chooses the slope of L3L_3L3​ to match L1L_1L1​'s, and uses the origin as the point that fixes its constant. 2
  • Checks whether L3L_3L3​ is a different line from L1L_1L1​ by comparing the two constants. 1

Part C 5

  • Gives a verdict for all three pairs, with the comparison behind each one shown. 3
  • Says which number each verdict rested on, and what the constants settle that a comparison of slopes cannot. 2

9. A form with three rules attached to it 14 points

Part A 5

  • Substitutes the point into point-slope form with the sign each subtraction imposes on a negative coordinate. 2
  • Clears the fractional slope by multiplying BOTH sides, so the equation stays balanced. 2
  • Delivers a form meeting all three conditions, and checks it against the given point. 1

Part B 4

  • Multiplies both sides by the denominator of the slope before distributing. 2
  • Gathers the terms onto the sides that leave the leading coefficient positive. 1
  • Checks the finished equation against the given point. 1

Part C 5

  • Identifies the one multiplier that would produce the requested coefficient, and says why no other could. 2
  • Applies that multiplier to the whole equation, both sides included, and writes out the result. 1
  • Tests the result against each of the three conditions and reaches a verdict naming the ones that fail. 2

10. A shortcut for reading a slope off standard form 17 points

Part A 5

  • Solves both equations for yyy, dividing every term and keeping the sign right when the coefficient of yyy is negative. 2
  • Computes the shortcut's two values separately, without quietly correcting them to the true ones. 2
  • Reports four numbers and says which two belong to the line and which two belong to the shortcut. 1

Part B 5

  • Applies the product test to the true slopes and reaches a verdict about the two lines. 2
  • Applies the same test to the shortcut's pair, kept separate from the true pair, and reports what it gives. 2
  • States plainly how the two verdicts stand to one another, and whether the two pairs of numbers do the same. 1

Part C 7

  • Names the omitted sign change as what goes wrong, and states the relationship between the shortcut's value and the true slope. 2
  • Shows why negating both slopes leaves the product test and the equality test unchanged, rather than only reporting that they did. 3
  • Separates the lines whose slope comes out wrong from those the shortcut happens to report correctly, and gives the reason for the exception; treating the vertical case separately is not a fault. 2
